article.title: Books for Software Engineers: 7 Ideas I Took From Them
article.h1: Books for Software Engineers: The Ideas I Took From My Reading
article.meta_description: A working engineer's list of books for software engineers: the seven books Lakshay Goyal read, the idea he kept from each, and how to use them at work.
article.intro: Books for software engineers do not have to be technical manuals. Lakshay Goyal's shelf is mostly non-technical: seven books on focus, freedom, courage and how to live. Below is each book, the idea he kept from it, and how that idea can shape everyday engineering work.
key_takeaways: Lakshay Goyal has read seven books, all listed on his bookshelf.
Most are non-technical: they cover focus, freedom, courage and empathy.
The 12 Week Year is the most directly useful book for planning work.
Technical lists add classics like Design Patterns and The Pragmatic Programmer.
Pair one technical book with one non-technical book for balance.

sections.heading: What books has Lakshay Goyal read?

blocks.text: Lakshay Goyal has read seven books that he keeps close: Freedom from the Known, The 12 Week Year, The Diary of a Young Girl, Krishna: The Man and His Philosophy, The Book of Man, The Book of Woman, and Why I Am an Atheist and Other Works. The full set lives on his bookshelf.

Lakshay is a Software Engineer building thoughtful mobile and web products. His bookshelf page describes the collection as ideas he keeps close: a small set of books he has read and the ideas he took from them.

blocks.caption: The seven books on the shelf and their authors
rows: The Diary of a Young Girl
Krishna: The Man and His Philosophy
Why I Am an Atheist and Other Works

blocks.text: You may notice that none of these is a programming book. That is on purpose. Most lists of books for developers stop at code, architecture and interviews. This one asks a different question: what else shapes how an engineer thinks, plans and treats people?

Six of the seven books are about people, belief and living well. Only one, The 12 Week Year, is about getting work done. That mix is the angle of this article, and it is why the list can sit next to any technical reading you already do.

sections.heading: What ideas did Lakshay Goyal take from these books?

blocks.text: Each book left one clear idea. Krishnamurti says your thoughts are second-hand, so look at life fresh. The 12 Week Year says treat every 12 weeks like a full year. Anne Frank shows hope under pressure. Bhagat Singh says to question everything, with logic and no ego.

blocks.caption: One idea per book, and where it can help an engineer
rows: Drop conditioning and look at life fresh
Treat every 12 weeks like a full year
The Diary of a Young Girl
Believe people are good at heart, even under pressure
Krishna: The Man and His Philosophy
Zorba the Buddha: enjoy life and stay aware
Love that tries to own someone is not love
Why I Am an Atheist and Other Works

blocks.text: The right-hand column is my reading of how each idea carries into software work. The middle column is what Lakshay took from the book. The next sections go through them one at a time, and each gives a small, practical way to use the idea.

blocks.alt: Stack of books showing a suggested reading order for software engineers
blocks.caption: A suggested reading order: start with the practical book, then move to the reflective ones.

blocks.text: If you only have time for two, start with The 12 Week Year for planning and Freedom from the Known for thinking. Together they cover how you decide what to build and how you decide how to build it.

sections.heading: Freedom from the Known: question what you inherited

blocks.text: Freedom from the Known, by J Krishnamurti, argues that your thoughts are second-hand and that you can drop the conditioning and look at life fresh. Lakshay says it messed with his head in a good way. For engineers, it is a book about assumptions.

Every codebase carries inherited decisions. A folder structure, a naming rule or a framework choice was once a fresh decision by someone else. Over time it becomes just how things are done. The book pushes you to ask whether the reason still holds.
How to use the idea in a project

items: Before copying a pattern, ask what problem it solved
Write down the assumption behind a design before you defend it
Read old code as if you had never seen the team's rules
Ask a newcomer which parts of the setup look odd to them

blocks.text: None of this means ignoring good practice. It means knowing why you follow it. When you can state the reason, you can also tell when the reason has gone away.
A small example

Say a team always builds a new service for every feature. Fresh eyes might ask whether a module inside the existing app would do. The answer may still be a new service. But the question is now a choice, not a habit, and that is the whole point of the book.

sections.heading: The 12 Week Year: plan in short cycles

blocks.text: The 12 Week Year, by Brian P. Moran and Michael Lennington, says to forget yearly goals and treat every 12 weeks like a full year. Lakshay calls it simple, and says it works against procrastination. It is the most directly practical book on his shelf.

A year is long enough to hide drift. You can lose a quarter and still feel on track. A 12-week window feels closer, so each week matters more. For engineers, this fits well with how product work already runs in cycles.
A simple 12-week loop

items: Pick one outcome for the next 12 weeks
Break it into goals for each week
Review progress at the end of every week
Adjust the plan based on what you learned
Start the next 12-week cycle with a fresh outcome

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Set 12-week outcome] --> B[Plan the week]
  B --> C[Do the work]
  C --> D[Weekly review]
  D --> B
  D --> E[Start new cycle]
blocks.alt: Flowchart of a repeating 12-week planning cycle with a weekly review step
blocks.caption: The 12-week loop: plan, work, review, repeat.

blocks.text: The weekly review is the part that makes it work. Without it, a plan is only a wish. With it, you notice slipping goals while there is still time to fix them.
Where it fits engineering work

Use it for learning goals, side projects or a large feature. Pick a clear outcome, such as shipping one working piece, then slice it into weekly tasks. If a week goes badly, you have eleven more weeks to adjust. That is easier to face than a missed yearly goal.

sections.heading: The Diary of a Young Girl, Krishna and Osho: staying steady

blocks.text: These four books are about staying steady and human under pressure. They give an engineer perspective more than technique. Each one gives a different answer to the same question: how do you keep your balance when things get hard?
The Diary of a Young Girl: keep perspective

Anne Frank's diary follows a 13-year-old hiding from the Nazis for two years, still believing people are good at heart. Lakshay says it makes his bad days look silly. A failed deploy or a rough review is real, but this book resets the scale.
Krishna: The Man and His Philosophy: calm in the middle of it

Osho presents Krishna as a man who danced, loved, fought and stayed calm through all of it. The lesson Lakshay took is that you do not need to run to the Himalayas to be spiritual. You can stay steady inside a busy life.
For engineers, that reads as on-call calm. You can care about the outcome and still keep a level head while debugging an incident.
The Book of Man: Zorba the Buddha

Osho looks at every role men get pushed into. The big takeaway is Zorba the Buddha: enjoy life fully and stay aware, with no need to pick one. In work terms, you can be driven and still be reflective. Ambition and awareness do not cancel each other.
The Book of Woman: love without ownership

This book is about love, freedom and the feminine side in all of us. Its sharpest point is that love that tries to own someone is not love. Lakshay says some takes you will love and some you will argue with. That is a fair way to read it.
Teams show this idea too. Good collaboration gives people room to own their work instead of controlling it.

sections.heading: Why I Am an Atheist and Other Works: question everything

blocks.text: Why I Am an Atheist and Other Works collects writing by Bhagat Singh. It shows a 23-year-old in jail, waiting to be hanged, calmly explaining why he does not believe in God. Lakshay describes it as zero ego and all logic, and the lesson is to question everything.
Engineers already value evidence. This book adds a standard for how to disagree: with reasons, calmly, and without making it personal. That is a useful bar for a design discussion.
Question everything, but do it with logic and without ego. That is a good rule for code review and for design.
Ways to apply it

items: Ask for the reason behind a requirement before building it
Disagree in review with evidence, not tone
Be ready to change your mind when the data says so
Say what you do not know instead of guessing

blocks.text: Pair this with Freedom from the Known. One tells you to look past inherited assumptions. The other shows how to challenge them calmly and clearly.

sections.heading: How do these compare with the usual technical lists?

blocks.text: Technical lists lean on classics. One list names Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann as its must-read, then A Philosophy of Software Design and The Pragmatic Programmer 20th Anniversary [S19]. These teach craft. The books above teach judgment, focus and temperament.

blocks.caption: Technical picks from other ranking lists
rows: Its ideas on replication, partitioning and transactions still map to modern systems [S21]
It explains 23 reusable approaches to recurring object-oriented design problems [S11]
Its advice is broad and general, and it covers concurrency, security and testing [S15]
A usability resource, now in its third edition with a mobile chapter [S2]
It offers 189 interview questions for practice [S1]
A long reference whose reasoning carries across most programming environments [S14]

blocks.text: These books are well loved for good reason. Lists like this are a fair place to start if you want to build skill in system design, patterns or interviews.
Why add non-technical books

Technical books tell you how to build. They rarely tell you how to decide what is worth building, how to stay steady under pressure, or how to disagree well. The books on Lakshay's shelf fill that gap, so they add to the technical classics instead of replacing them.
A reading order that mixes both

items: Start with a practical technical book such as The Pragmatic Programmer
Add The 12 Week Year to plan your reading and your work
Read Freedom from the Known to question your habits
Move on to a deeper technical book like Designing Data-Intensive Applications
Finish with a reflective title such as Why I Am an Atheist and Other Works

blocks.text: One list suggests early-career engineers begin with The Pragmatic Programmer and later move to Designing Data-Intensive Applications at mid-level [S22][S23]. Slot a non-technical book between each step to keep the reading balanced.

Books for software engineers work best when you pick a few and actually apply them. Start with the full bookshelf to see each book with the idea Lakshay took from it, then choose one to read this month.
For more notes from building and deploying software, browse the blog. To see the work behind the reading, visit the about page and learn what keeps Lakshay curious.
If you want to talk about books, products or engineering, the contact link on the site lets you book a 30-minute chat.

faq.question: Are non-technical books worth reading for engineers?
faq.answer: Yes. Lakshay Goyal's shelf is mostly non-technical, and the ideas on focus, planning and questioning assumptions apply to daily engineering work. Pair them with a technical classic for balance.

faq.question: Which book is best for planning work?
faq.answer: The 12 Week Year. Lakshay says its idea of treating every 12 weeks like a full year stops procrastination. It is simple, and it works.

faq.question: Which book helps most with questioning assumptions?
faq.answer: Freedom from the Known by J Krishnamurti. It argues that your thoughts are second-hand and asks you to look at life fresh, which helps when you review inherited code or habits.

sources.passage: Cracking the Coding Interview by Gayle Laakmann McDowell is one of the best books for software engineer aspirants who want to improve their chances of acing a job interview. From her experience interviewing and coaching countless software engineers, McDowell created a book with 189 real-world interview questions to help you practice. The book also includes handy tips and five tried-and-tested strategies proven to help you answer similar questions and come

sources.title: 10 Best Software Engineering Books to Read in 2026
sources.passage: Don’t Make Me Think is a book by Steve Krug, a usability guru who also happens to be an expert on information design and intuitive navigation. The book’s first edition came out in 2000 and has since been a beneficial resource for those looking to learn more about UX (user experience) design. It is currently on its third edition, which has been updated to include a chapter covering mobile usability.

sources.title: 10 BEST Software Engineering Books (2026 Update)
sources.passage: The case studies show how code improves through repeated cleanup. Published in 2008, the book uses Java for most of its examples, so readers working in other languages will need to translate some details. Treat the rules as discussion points rather than laws, and compare the advice with your team’s own standards.

sources.title: 10 BEST Software Engineering Books (2026 Update)
sources.passage: Design Patterns by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides explains 23 reusable approaches to recurring object-oriented design problems. Each pattern describes its purpose, structure, participants, and likely effects, giving teams a common vocabulary for discussing design.

sources.title: 10 BEST Software Engineering Books (2026 Update)
sources.passage: This is a reference book rather than a step-by-step course. Published in 2002, it illustrates its patterns with Java and C# examples, and the architecture problems it describes still appear in current systems. Readers need experience with databases and application design. Use your framework’s documentation when turning a pattern into production code.

sources.title: 10 BEST Software Engineering Books (2026 Update)
sources.passage: The pattern language is still useful for queues, event systems, and integration platforms. Published in 2003, its examples use JMS, .NET messaging, and XML-based tools, so pair it with the documentation for the broker or cloud service you use. This is a dense reference for readers who already know distributed systems.

sources.title: 10 BEST Software Engineering Books (2026 Update)
sources.passage: At 960 pages, the second edition is long, and its examples use C++, Java, and Visual Basic, but its reasoning carries across most programming environments. Beginners can read selected chapters, while experienced developers can use it as a reference. Readers seeking framework-specific guidance will need another source beside it.

sources.title: 10 BEST Software Engineering Books (2026 Update)
sources.passage: The advice is broad, so it will not replace a language guide or an architecture reference. Its strength is helping readers question how they work. This 20th Anniversary Edition, published in 2019, also covers concurrency, security, and testing, and its lessons are intentionally general so each team can adapt them.

sources.title: 10 BEST Software Engineering Books (2026 Update)
sources.passage: This is the outlier in a software engineering list because it explains AI concepts rather than software construction. It can help developers understand product discussions and limits, but it will not teach production machine learning. Published in 2018, it works best as a grounding in core ideas such as data, algorithms, and machine learning rather than a guide to current AI tools.
